item.title: Vicksburg police address community concerns after Tommy’s BBQ robbery - Darkhorse Press
item.author: Morgan Howard
item.description:
VICKSBURG – The Vicksburg Police Department is clarifying details about a medical call involving the person accused in a robbery at Tommy’s BBQ after receiving multiple calls from the public.

Police said concerns had been raised about whether the individual was in Vicksburg police custody earlier the same day before the robbery.

According to VPD, 911 dispatch received a call around 6 p.m. Saturday, May 16, requesting a mental or medical evaluation for an individual reportedly exhibiting unusual behavior, including talking to stop signs and sweating heavily.

Fire Medic 30, Engine 6 and a Vicksburg police officer were dispatched to the scene. Police said the officer responded to provide routine scene security and standby support because of the nature of the call.

According to a review of 911 calls, radio traffic and related records, the individual was not reported to be a threat to himself or others and was not reported to have any weapons.

Police said the responding officer made routine contact with the individual and asked standard questions related to the medical call and the person’s well-being. Once the individual entered the ambulance, police said he remained calm and did not exhibit disruptive behavior.

The officer then cleared the scene and returned to service without incident.

The individual was taken by Fire Medic 30 to Merit Health River Region without incident. Police said that, based on the information reviewed, the individual became disruptive after arriving at the hospital, and EMS requested assistance from sheriff’s deputies.

VPD said the individual was not in the custody of the Vicksburg Police Department before the robbery and did not show disruptive or uncooperative behavior that would have warranted detention during the initial medical call.

The department said the clarification was released to provide transparency and address community concerns about the timeline of events.

item.title: Suspect arrested after fraudulent check reported at Tupelo bank - Darkhorse Press
item.author: Morgan Howard
item.description:
TUPELO – A suspect was arrested after police said someone attempted to cash a fraudulent check at a Tupelo bank.

According to the Tupelo Police Department, officers responded May 20 to BNA Bank, located at 3041 McCullough Blvd., in reference to a false pretense report.

When officers arrived, bank employees told police a suspect had attempted to cash a fraudulent check and left the business.

Officers were able to locate the suspect nearby, and the suspect was taken into custody.

item.title: Rankin County K-9 medically retired after collapsing during search for escaped juvenile - Darkhorse Press
item.author: Therese Apel
item.description:
RANKIN COUNTY — A Rankin County Sheriff’s Office K-9 deputy has been medically retired after collapsing during a search Thursday afternoon for an escaped juvenile offender in Pelahatchie.

According to the Rankin County Sheriff’s Office, Deputy Ronnie Decell and his K-9 partner, Fox, responded May 21 to assist in locating a juvenile who had escaped from the Rankin County Juvenile Detention Center.

Officials said Deputy Decell deployed Fox to track the suspect, but about 100 yards into the search, the dog suddenly collapsed.

Deputy Decell carried Fox back to his patrol vehicle and rushed him to the after-hours emergency veterinary clinic URGIVET in Madison for treatment.

Veterinarians later determined Fox was suffering from an undiagnosed tumor that ruptured during the track, causing severe internal bleeding near his heart, according to the sheriff’s office.

Fox remains under treatment and observation for what officials described as a life-threatening condition. Because of the diagnosis, the sheriff’s office said Fox will be medically retired from service.

Fox, a 10-year-old Belgian Malinois, is trained and certified in narcotics detection, tracking and handler protection. The sheriff’s office said he has served Rankin County throughout his career alongside Deputy Decell.

Sheriff Bryan Bailey asked the community to keep Deputy Decell, his family and Fox in their thoughts and prayers.

item.title: Mississippi Museum of Natural Science offering free admission to military families through Blue Star Museums program - Darkhorse Press
item.author: Therese Apel
item.description:
JACKSON — The Mississippi Department of Wildlife, Fisheries, and Parks announced that the Mississippi Museum of Natural Science is participating in the 2026 Blue Star Museums program, offering free admission to active-duty military personnel and their families through Sept. 7.

The program allows currently serving members of the U.S. military and up to five family members to visit the museum free of charge during the summer.

Museum officials said military families will have access to exhibits, wildlife displays, scenic trails and outdoor experiences at the museum and nearby LeFleur’s Bluff State Park.

“We are honored to welcome military families to the Mississippi Museum of Natural Science through the Blue Star Museums program,” said Angel Rohnke. “This initiative is a meaningful way to thank those who serve our country while providing opportunities for families to connect with Mississippi’s natural resources, conservation and outdoor recreation.”

Blue Star Museums is a partnership involving the National Endowment for the Arts, Blue Star Families, the Department of Defense and museums across the country.

Eligible participants include active-duty members of the Army, Marine Corps, Navy, Air Force, Space Force and Coast Guard, as well as members of the Reserves, National Guard, U.S. Public Health Commissioned Corps and NOAA Commissioned Corps.

Visitors must present a qualifying military identification card for admission. Accepted forms of ID include a Common Access Card, DD Form 1173 dependent ID card, DD Form 1173-1 ID card or a Next Generation Uniformed Services ID card.

More information about the program and participating museums is available at Blue Star Museums.

item.title: Mississippi Highway Patrol to increase enforcement for Memorial Day travel period - Darkhorse Press
item.author: Morgan Howard
item.description:
JACKSON – The Mississippi Highway Patrol is preparing for the summer travel season by increasing enforcement during the Memorial Day holiday travel period.

The enforcement period will begin at 6 p.m. Friday, May 22, and end at midnight Monday, May 25.

MHP said the Memorial Day holiday travel period coincides with the national “Click It or Ticket” safety campaign. Troopers will place emphasis on Mississippi’s occupant restraint laws, along with enforcement of speeding, distracted driving and impaired driving laws.

Safety checkpoints will also be used throughout the weekend in an effort to reduce crashes.

“As we honor the brave men and women who gave their lives for our country this Memorial Day, let’s also do our part to protect the lives around us,” Commissioner Sean Tindell said. “If you’re traveling this weekend, buckle up, slow down, and never drive impaired. One safe decision can save a life.”

During the 2025 Memorial Day holiday travel period, MHP investigated 137 crashes with six fatalities on state and federal highway systems. Troopers also made 73 DUI arrests and issued 592 citations for occupant restraint violations.

item.title: Louisville man sentenced in federal fentanyl trafficking case - Darkhorse Press
item.author: Therese Apel
item.description:
ABERDEEN — A Louisville man will serve more than four years in federal prison after pleading guilty in a fentanyl trafficking case, according to federal officials.

Medford Delon Eiland, 39, was sentenced to 51 months in prison and five years of supervised release after pleading guilty to conspiracy to distribute and possession with intent to distribute more than 40 grams of fentanyl. Senior U.S. District Judge Sharion Aycock handed down the sentence.

According to court records, a suspicious Priority Express Mail package mailed from Tolleson, Arizona, to Eiland’s Louisville address was intercepted by a U.S. Postal Inspection Service inspector on March 7, 2022. After obtaining a federal search warrant, investigators opened the package and found a heat-sealed bag containing numerous blue pills.

Because of the danger of fentanyl exposure, authorities removed the pills before conducting a controlled delivery to the residence. After the package was delivered, officers with the United States Postal Inspection Service, Mississippi Bureau of Narcotics, Mississippi Highway Patrol and Winston County Sheriff’s Office approached the home.

Officials said Eiland fled into a wooded area behind the residence but was later located and detained. Authorities said Eiland admitted he knew the package contained narcotics, though he claimed he did not know it contained fentanyl.

Investigators estimated the package contained about 500 dosage units, and laboratory testing confirmed the pills contained fentanyl. Authorities also found Eiland’s fingerprints on the parcel.

U.S. Attorney Scott Leary said fentanyl has “devastated families and destroyed communities” and pledged continued prosecution of traffickers.

Robert Eikhoff said the quantity of fentanyl pills “would have continued poisoning our communities and destroying lives.”

Federal officials said the case was prosecuted as part of the Homeland Security Task Force initiative, a multiagency effort targeting cartels, gangs and drug trafficking organizations.

Assistant U.S. Attorney Sam Stringfellow prosecuted the case.

item.title: Leake County deputies seize meth, firearms during drug bust - Darkhorse Press
item.author: Morgan Howard
item.description:
LEAKE COUNTY – A large amount of drugs and several firearms were seized during a drug bust in Leake County, according to the Leake County Sheriff’s Office.

Sheriff Randy W. Atkinson said deputies and investigators seized 395 grams of methamphetamine, 54 grams of spice, 10 grams of marijuana and five firearms from a home off Pearl Hill Road.

According to the sheriff’s office, the methamphetamine seized was 58 grams shy of a pound and had an estimated street value of $5,000.

One person was taken into custody during the operation. The sheriff’s office did not immediately release the person’s name or charges.

No injuries were reported during the arrest, and officials said public safety remained the top priority throughout the operation.

The sheriff’s office is encouraging anyone with information about drug activity to contact deputies.

item.title: Lawrence County sheriff warns residents after recent burglaries - Darkhorse Press
item.author: Morgan Howard
item.description:
LAWRENCE COUNTY -vThe Lawrence County Sheriff’s Office is urging residents to secure their homes and vehicles after several burglaries were reported over the past week.

Sheriff Ryan Everett said the county had gone a long time without a residential or vehicle burglary, but deputies have recently investigated one residential burglary, one attempted residential burglary and two automobile burglaries.

Everett encouraged residents to lock their homes and vehicles and avoid leaving valuables in plain sight. He also reminded people to keep records of important property, including brands, model numbers, calibers and serial numbers, so items can be more easily identified if stolen.

The sheriff also urged residents to practice firearm safety, including treating every gun as if it is loaded.

Everett warned those committing burglaries that there would be no sympathy from his office and encouraged them to change course before facing serious consequences.

The sheriff’s office is asking residents to remain alert and take steps to protect their property.

item.title: Cleveland men sentenced in federal gun cases after convenience store shootout - Darkhorse Press
item.author: Therese Apel
item.description:
OXFORD — Two Cleveland men have been sentenced in separate federal gun cases stemming from a shootout at a local convenience store, according to federal officials.

Jamarcus Miller, 38, was sentenced Thursday by Chief U.S. District Judge Debra M. Brown to 80 months in federal prison after previously pleading guilty to possessing ammunition as a convicted felon.

Earlier this year, Senior U.S. District Judge Michael P. Mills sentenced Jamario Hodges, 32, to 70 months in prison followed by three years of supervised release after he pleaded guilty to being a felon in possession of a firearm.

According to court records, the ammunition tied to Miller was recovered after officers with the Cleveland Police Department responded to a shooting at a convenience store in Cleveland. Surveillance video allegedly showed Miller and Hodges exchanging gunfire near gas pumps before fleeing the scene.

Investigators recovered shell casings from the area where Miller was allegedly shooting. When officers later located Hodges, authorities said he was carrying a firearm equipped with a Glock switch, an illegal device that converts a handgun into a fully automatic weapon.

Federal officials said both men were convicted felons at the time of the shooting and were separately indicted by a federal grand jury before pleading guilty.

Miller and Hodges also face state charges related to the shooting in Bolivar County Circuit Court, where those cases remain pending.

U.S. Attorney Scott Leary said violent offenders “put innocent people in danger” and pledged continued cooperation between federal and local agencies to remove violent criminals from the streets.

Robert Eikhoff said the shooting “instilled fear and put innocent members of the community at risk.”

The case was investigated by the Federal Bureau of Investigation, the Cleveland Police Department and the United States Marshals Service. Assistant U.S. Attorney Julie Addison prosecuted the case.

item.title: 14-year-old captured after climbing fence during recreation at juvenile detention center - Darkhorse Press
item.author: Morgan Howard
item.description:
RANKIN COUNTY – A 14-year-old juvenile detainee was captured Thursday night after escaping from the Rankin County Juvenile Detention Center and later leading deputies on a pursuit in a stolen vehicle.

According to the Rankin County Sheriff’s Office, officers at the detention center reported around 3 p.m. May 21 that a juvenile detainee had escaped from the facility in Pelahatchie after climbing a security fence and running away.

Sheriff Bryan Bailey said detainees were participating in mandatory outdoor recreation, with several playing basketball, when the basketball rolled near the perimeter fence. The juvenile ran toward the ball and began climbing the 16-foot security fence.

A detention officer responded and grabbed the juvenile while he was on the fence, attempting to pull him back down. The sheriff’s office said the juvenile broke free, climbed over the fence and ran into a wooded area.

Deputies and assisting law enforcement agencies responded and established a perimeter. Rankin County Sheriff’s Office K-9 units, Flowood Police Department K-9 units, Mississippi Highway Patrol K-9 units and the sheriff’s office drone team assisted in the search.

Authorities said an extensive ground and aerial search continued through the afternoon and evening, and checkpoints were set up in the surrounding area.

Around 11 p.m., a Banks Street resident called 911 and reported that the escapee was at her home attempting to steal her husband’s white Chevrolet 2500 pickup truck. The caller said the juvenile left the residence traveling west on Highway 80 toward Brandon.

Deputies soon located the stolen vehicle and attempted a traffic stop, but the juvenile refused to stop, leading deputies on a pursuit that lasted about 20 minutes and traveled along several county roads.

Deputies attempted to direct the pursuit toward Brandon, where Brandon police had deployed stop sticks. The juvenile eventually turned onto Mount Ridge Road, a dead-end road, where deputies were able to box in the vehicle.

Authorities said the juvenile then attempted to escape through a cutover area but became stuck. Deputies reached the vehicle and took him into custody before he could run away again.

Pafford Ambulance Service responded and transported the juvenile to a local hospital for treatment of injuries sustained during the escape. After treatment, he was returned to the custody of the Rankin County Juvenile Detention Center.

The sheriff’s office said the stolen vehicle sustained heavy damage. The owner operates a small landscaping business and relies on the truck for work.

The juvenile was originally being held at the detention center on charges of auto theft and auto burglary. He is scheduled to appear before Youth Court Judge Josh McCrory.

The Rankin County Juvenile Detention Center opened in 2011, and officials said this was the first escape in the facility’s history. Bailey and McCrory are reevaluating outdoor recreation security procedures and plan to implement additional measures while staying in compliance with state and federal guidelines for juvenile detention facilities.

Bailey thanked deputies, dispatchers, detention officers and assisting agencies, including the Mississippi Highway Patrol, Pelahatchie Police Department, Flowood Police Department, Brandon Police Department, Madison Police Department and Scott County Sheriff’s Department.

“We hope the quick recapture of this escapee provides peace of mind to our citizens,” Bailey said.

item.title: Venezuelan man with alleged Tren de Aragua ties sentenced in ATM fraud scheme - Darkhorse Press
item.author: Therese Apel
item.description:
NORTH MISSISSIPPI — A Venezuelan man federal prosecutors say has ties to the international gang Tren de Aragua was sentenced Wednesday in Oxford for his role in a bank fraud conspiracy involving ATM “jackpotting” schemes across Mississippi.

Darrin Daza-Segura, 26, who was living in Dallas as an undocumented immigrant, was sentenced by U.S. District Judge Michael P. Mills to 10 months in federal prison followed by three years of supervised release. He was also ordered to pay $47,250 in restitution.

According to court documents, Daza-Segura will be turned over to U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement custody for removal proceedings following his prison sentence and will not be permitted to re-enter the country without authorization from the Department of Homeland Security.

Federal prosecutors said Daza-Segura and co-defendant Winder Alexander Canelon-Tiapa traveled throughout Mississippi reprogramming ATMs to force machines to dispense large amounts of cash, a crime commonly referred to as “ATM jackpotting.” Authorities said the pair successfully stole approximately $47,000 and attempted to steal more from banks across the state.

Federal authorities nationwide have linked similar “ATM jackpotting” schemes to alleged members of Tren de Aragua, who investigators say use malware to force ATMs to release cash.

U.S. Attorney Scott Leary said the defendants targeted communities in north Mississippi while traveling through the region.

“These Venezuelan gang members have been categorized as terrorists,” Leary said in a statement. “They do not live here but have come to victimize our citizens in North Mississippi.”

Mississippi Attorney General Lynn Fitch said investigators were able to stop a “dangerous TdA gang member from defrauding Mississippians.”

The case was investigated by the Cyber Crime Division of the Mississippi Attorney General’s Office and is being prosecuted by Assistant U.S. Attorney Clayton A. Dabbs.

item.title: Police investigating attempted shooting, robbery at Southaven Walmart - Darkhorse Press
item.author: Therese Apel
item.description:
SOUTHAVEN — Police are investigating after a robbery and attempted shooting were reported Thursday evening in the parking lot of a Walmart in Southaven.

According to the Southaven Police Department, officers responded around 7:15 p.m. to reports of shots fired in the west parking lot of the store.

Investigators said preliminary information indicates a suspect robbed the victim and then attempted to shoot him before fleeing the area.

No injuries were reported.

Police said responding officers secured the scene and there is no ongoing threat to the business or the public.

The investigation remains active.

Investigators said preliminary information indicates a suspect robbed the victim and then attempted to shoot him before fleeing the area.

No injuries were reported.

Police said responding officers secured the scene and there is no ongoing threat to the business or the public.

The investigation remains active.

item.title: MDWFP, National Park Service to Host Free Youth Fish Camp in June - Darkhorse Press
item.author: Therese Apel
item.description:
JACKSON — The Mississippi Department of Wildlife, Fisheries, and Parks Visitor Education Center at the Bob Tyler Fish Hatchery is partnering with the National Park Service to host a free fish camp for youth ages 10 to 15 on June 10.

The camp will run from 9 a.m. to 3 p.m. and will introduce participants to fishing basics, hatchery operations and the National Park Service Junior Angler Program.

According to MDWFP, campers will learn fish identification, water safety tips and participate in catfish fishing at the hatchery’s Visitor Education Center pond. Youth will also tour the hatchery, meet a National Park Service ranger and learn more about earning the National Park Service Junior Angler Badge.

Fishing equipment and bait will be provided during the event. Participants who complete the full day of activities will receive special items and earn the Junior Angler Badge.

The program is free, but pre-registration is required. Those interested can call the Visitor Education Center at 662-563-8068 or email [email protected] to request a registration form.

The Visitor Education Center is part of the Bob Tyler Fish Hatchery and is located off Interstate 55 at Exit 233 east.

item.title: LEO training board approves new pathway for part-time officers to earn full-time certification - Darkhorse Press
item.author: Therese Apel
item.description:
PEARL — Part-time law enforcement officers in Mississippi will have a new pathway to full-time certification under a rule approved this week by the Board of Law Enforcement Officers Standards and Training.

BLEOST approved Rule 9.5 for filing with the Secretary of State’s Office, establishing an alternative route for currently certified part-time officers to obtain full-time certification through demonstrated competency, training equivalency and sustained service — without completing a traditional full-time academy.

Under the rule, officers who have already completed an approved part-time training program may pursue full-time certification through evaluations conducted by accredited full-time training academies. The rule must complete the formal approval process with the Secretary of State before taking effect. Public Safety Commissioner Sean Tindell said the rule addresses a practical barrier that has kept qualified officers from advancing.

“I’m proud of the work being done to help part-time officers establish full-time certification opportunities for those who want to serve and protect their communities, but may not have the time or financial ability to step away from their other jobs to attend a traditional full-time academy,” Tindell said.

Lee County Sheriff Jim H. Johnson called the rule a meaningful step for agencies struggling to fill full-time positions.

“This is a great change to help our part-time officers achieve full-time status through the proper evaluation and training process that needs to be done to help increase our public safety in local communities across the state,” Johnson said.

BLEOST credited Standards and Training Director Vanderford and Harrison County Sheriff’s Office Captain Hendry with developing and presenting the rule to the board.

item.title: June 18 verdict scheduled in Quinton Tellis murder trial - Darkhorse Press
item.author: Therese Apel
item.description:
MONROE, La. — Closing arguments concluded Thursday in the bench trial of Quinton Tellis, charged with the 2015 murder of Ming Chen “Mandy” Hsiao, with the state painting a portrait of a calculated killer who tortured his victim for her PIN number and the defense arguing the case against their client amounts to little more than supposition built on a foundation of circumstantial evidence.

Judge Larry Jefferson will issue his ruling June 18 at 9 a.m. in Ouachita Parish court.

ADA Holly Jones opened her closing argument by returning to the theme she established at the outset of trial: that Mandy Hsiao was killed by a person devoid of emotion who wanted one thing, her money. She framed the case as a blank canvas filled in fact by fact until the full picture became undeniable.

“When using your reason and common sense, and looking at the existence of all of these facts, such facts will exclude any reasonable hypothesis of the defendant’s innocence,” Jones told Judge Jefferson.

Jones walked the court methodically through three distinct time periods: what investigators knew before Tellis’s first interview on August 11, 2015; what they learned between that interview and his second on August 19th; and what came to light after his arrest. At each stage, she argued, the evidence that emerged contradicted what Tellis had told police. And he had told police, repeatedly and emphatically, that he was telling the truth.

“I’m telling the truth, that I’m going to be straightforward and honest with you. I swear to God, I ain’t got no reason to lie to you. God can kill me right now, and I’m not lying about nothing. That’s on my grandma’s graveyard,” Jones quoted from his August 11th statement, before methodically laying out everything he had omitted from that interview: numerous Chase Bank calls, the fact that he knew Hsiao’s PIN number, the attempt to use Mohammed Mahrous as a money mule, the Vicksburg ATM withdrawals and his assertion that it wasn’t him in the surveillance photos of him, the Exxon receipt found in his home.

Jones saved her sharpest argument for the four phone calls made between 8:16 and 8:18 p.m. on July 29, 2015, two from Mandy’s iPhone and two from Tellis’s Nokia, all to the same Chase automated banking number, all within the same two-minute window. She noted that in six previous calls to Chase in May, Mandy had never once dialed a 1 before the 800 number. She knew she didn’t have to. On July 29th, both calls from her phone included the 1, because, Jones argued, whoever was dialing was reading the number off the back of the debit card, where it is printed with a 1 in front.

“The fact that the four phone calls occurred within the same minute, with the first two being made using Mandy’s cellular phone and the last two being made using the defendant’s cell phone, places Mandy and the defendant together at that point in time without question,” Jones said. “How do we know this? Because on August 8th, when they took all the evidence out of Mandy’s apartment, Mandy’s cell phone was still in the apartment.”

Jones argued that the presence of Mandy’s phone in the apartment on August 8th, combined with its use on the night of July 29th simultaneous with Tellis’s phone, left only one conclusion: he was there. And if he was there and left her alive, Jones said, there was no explaining what came next.

“If he allowed her to live, why in the world would she not immediately pick up the phone and call the police?” Jones said. “Because she was dead. Because he killed her. There is no other reasonable hypothesis.”

Jones addressed the DNA evidence directly, conceding there was none linking Tellis to the scene, but arguing the state of Mandy’s body after 10 days of decomposition in the Louisiana heat would have destroyed whatever was there. She also characterized the Y chromosome found in a rectal swab as not a DNA profile and not evidence of sexual assault, calling it a potential red herring, and noted that 17 people had their DNA tested in connection with the case and none were connected to the scene either.

On the testimony of Eric Hill, Tellis’s wife’s cousin who said Tellis called him from jail and told him to find someone to blame for Mandy’s murder, Jones argued Hill’s knowledge of details that were never made public, including the number and nature of the stab wounds, could only have come from Tellis himself. She acknowledged Hill had told multiple stories but said Detective Duane Cookson’s corroboration of the non-public details was the verification the court needed.

Jones closed by returning to the simplest question in the case. Mandy Hsiao sent a Facebook message at 7:41 p.m. on July 29, 2015. After that, nothing: no calls, no texts, no banking, no social media, no sign of life of any kind until her body was found on August 8th.

“What person in today’s society, especially a relatively young person, goes without making a cell phone call, making a text, signing onto Wi-Fi, looking at Instagram, checking Facebook? She didn’t touch nothing. Nothing was accessed after that time. She’s dead. And he did it.”

Defense attorney Bob Noel offered a sharply different reading of the same evidence, arguing the state had spent the entire trial trafficking in possibilities rather than proof.

“I’ve never been in a murder case where everything is supposition, guesswork, assumed as this case,” he told Judge Jefferson. “We’re in the proof business, Your Honor, and they haven’t proved anything.”

Noel challenged the timeline Jones had constructed around Katelyn Hearn’s testimony, putting heavy emphasis that Hearn had told police at one point that she heard a thud in Mandy’s bedroom and she thought it could have been between 9 and 9:30 p.m., not around 7:45 as the state suggested, and that she admitted on cross-examination it could have been as late as 8:06 p.m. before she arrived home. He also questioned whether Mandy was even home before her phone connected to a neighbor’s Wi-Fi at 8:13, noting that Facebook Messenger can be accessed from anywhere.

On the four phone calls, Noel suggested a scenario in which Mandy, having just discovered her card was missing, called Chase at the same moment Tellis was calling to access the account. He argued Tellis could have obtained the card any number of ways without ever entering her apartment, and could have seen her PIN when she used her card at Walmart, or she may have had her notebook with her containing the number.

“We have no burden to show how he got it,” Noel said. “They have the burden to prove how he got it.”

The absence of physical evidence was the cornerstone of the defense argument. No DNA belonging to Tellis was found anywhere in Mandy’s apartment. No blood was found in his car despite a Blue Star reagent test. No blood-stained clothing was ever recovered. Noel noted that those facts applied equally to every other person whose DNA was tested, and none of them were charged with murder.

Noel reserved his most pointed attack for Eric Hill, calling him the state’s star witness and arguing the entire murder case collapsed without him. He catalogued Hill’s shifting stories, four by his count, and highlighted what he called the ultimate lie: Hill’s claim to have testified at a prior Tellis trial. No such trial existed, Noel said.

“He has no credibility, Your Honor. Without him, they’ve got nothing but yet they’re guessing.”

Jones countered in rebuttal that Hill had been subpoenaed and present for a preliminary hearing and may have confused the terminology, and that his knowledge of non-public details about Mandy’s injuries was corroboration enough. She pointed out that Tellis had at least 10 days to dispose of any blood evidence between the time when Mandy was killed and when her body was discovered, even before he was first questioned on August 11.

Noel closed by invoking the Jackson v. Virginia standard, arguing that even viewing the evidence in the light most favorable to the state, the prosecution had not proven beyond a reasonable doubt that Quinton Tellis committed this murder.

Jones had the final word in rebuttal, returning to the four phone calls, the missing debit card, the silence that followed July 29th, and the question she said had no reasonable answer.

“There is no one else connected to Mandy and that credit card except for the defendant. There is no one else that was at that apartment with her on July 29th,” she said.

“The biggest tell-all is no electronic footprint after July 29th, 2015. She’s dead. And he did it.”

Judge Larry Jefferson will issue his ruling June 18 at 9 a.m. in Ouachita Parish.

item.title: Genuine MS Farmers Market moving to Brandon Amphitheater after strong opening turnout - Darkhorse Press
item.author: Therese Apel
item.description:
BRANDON — The Genuine MS Farmers Market in Brandon is moving to a new location after large crowds during its opening weekend quickly exceeded parking capacity, state officials announced.

Mississippi Agriculture Commissioner Andy Gipson said the seasonal market will begin operating Saturday, May 23, at the Brandon Amphitheater, located at 8190 Rock Way.

Gipson said the decision was made following an “incredibly positive public response” to the market’s debut.

“We are excited to relocate the Genuine MS Farmers Market to the Brandon Amphitheater,” Gipson said in a statement. “This move will also allow the market to grow by adding more vendors as we head into the summer season.”

Brandon Mayor Butch Lee said the city welcomed the move to improve traffic flow and public convenience after the successful opening weekend at the Rankin County Co-op.

“We look forward to seeing everyone there,” Lee said.

Officials said the new location offers better access, additional parking and more room for vendors and shoppers.

The market features vendors selling Mississippi-grown, Mississippi-raised and Mississippi-processed products, including produce, meat, dairy items, honey, plants and specialty foods.

The market is scheduled to operate every Saturday from 8 a.m. until noon through October, weather permitting.

Gipson also thanked the Rankin County Co-op for hosting the market’s opening weekend and said the department hopes to partner with the co-op for future events.

Farmers and producers interested in becoming vendors can contact the Mississippi Department of Agriculture and Commerce at [email protected] or by calling 601-354-6573.

item.title: Flooding closes select clinics at G.V. Sonny Montgomery VA Medical Center - Darkhorse Press
item.author: Morgan Howard
item.description:
JACKSON – Several specialty clinics at the G.V. Sonny Montgomery VA Medical Center were closed Thursday because of flooding.

The closures were announced for the remainder of Thursday, May 21, to ensure the safety of veterans, visitors and staff. Officials said all other clinics, including primary care and other specialty clinic appointments, are continuing as scheduled at this time.

The affected clinics include Women’s Health, also known as the Pink Clinic, Cardiology, Dermatology, Renal, Spinal Cord and Gastroenterology.

Veterans with appointments in those clinics will be contacted directly by staff to move appointments to virtual visits when appropriate or to reschedule for the next available appointment time.

Veterans with appointments outside the affected clinics should continue reporting for care as planned unless they are contacted directly by VA staff.

Anyone with questions about their care or upcoming appointments may contact the Clinical Contact Center at 601-362-4471.

Officials said teams are working to safely address the flooding and restore normal operations.

item.title: Deputies searching for male who fled Rankin County Youth Court building - Darkhorse Press
item.author: Morgan Howard
item.description:
RANKIN COUNTY – Rankin County deputies are searching for a man who ran from the Rankin County Youth Court building shortly after 3 p.m., according to Rankin County Investigator Tyler Burnell.

Burnell said a deputy assigned to Rankin County Youth Court contacted 911 dispatch by police radio and reported that he was in a foot pursuit with a male who was trying to flee the building.

Officials said there is no risk to juveniles at the facility.

Deputies are currently searching an area north of Highway 80.

No additional information was immediately available.
